Dove (Doctrine)
DUV
n.
Old English dūfe; Hebrew yōnāh (dove, including the rock dove and turtledove); Greek peristera (dove). One of the most extensive bird-metaphors in Scripture, including Noah’s dove, the dove of the Holy Spirit at Christ’s baptism, the dove of the Song of Solomon, and the sacrificial doves of the poor.

📖 Biblical Definition

The dove is one of the most extensive bird-metaphors in Scripture, governing several distinct theological registers. First, Noah’s dove (Gen 8:8-12). In the flood-narrative’s climactic scene, Noah sends out a dove from the ark to see if the waters had abated. The first time, she returns without finding rest for her foot; the second time, she returns with an olive leaf plucked off in her mouth, the sign that the waters were receding; the third time, she returns no more. The dove with the olive-leaf is one of Scripture’s most enduring symbols of peace and renewal—the post-judgment promise of God’s peace with His creation after the waters of judgment have receded. Second, the dove of the Holy Spirit at Christ’s baptism (Matt 3:16; Mark 1:10; Luke 3:22; John 1:32). At the inauguration of Christ’s ministry, the Holy Spirit descends visibly upon Him in a bodily shape like a dove, accompanied by the Father’s voice from heaven: this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. The dove-form is theologically significant: gentleness, peace, the heavenly origin (descending from heaven), and the harkening-back of post-flood-renewal imagery (the dove signaling new creation). The Holy Spirit’s dove-descent at Christ’s baptism inaugurates the new-creation work the Spirit will accomplish through Christ’s ministry. Third, the dove of the Song of Solomon, the great love-poem of Scripture, repeatedly addresses the beloved as the dove: my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely (Song 2:14); my dove, my undefiled, is but one (Song 6:9). The dove-imagery serves the love-poem’s tender intimacy, with the church’s typological echo as the dove of Christ. Fourth, the sacrificial doves of the poor. Leviticus 12:8; 14:22; 15:14, 29 prescribe pairs of turtledoves or young pigeons as the burnt-and-sin offerings the poor could substitute when they could not afford a lamb. Mary and Joseph offered two turtledoves at the temple after Mary’s purification (Luke 2:24), indicating their economic poverty—a small but significant detail in the Gospel narrative. Fifth, the dove’s wisdom-and-innocence pairing in Christ’s instruction to His disciples (Matt 10:16): behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves. The dove’s harmlessness is paired with the serpent’s wisdom as the model for the disciple sent forth in hostile territory. The dove therefore carries a remarkable range of biblical meaning: post-judgment peace and new creation (Noah); the heavenly anointing and the inauguration of Christ’s ministry (Christ’s baptism); the tender intimacy of covenant love (Song of Solomon); the offering of the poor (Levitical worship); the harmless-with-the-wise disposition of the discipleship-witness (Matt 10:16).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DOVE as a fowl of the genus Columba; in scripture, the bird of Noah’s flood-narrative (Gen 8), the visible form of the Holy Spirit’s descent at Christ’s baptism (Matt 3:16; Luke 3:22), the address of the beloved in the Song of Solomon, the offering of the poor in Leviticus, and the model of harmless-with-wise discipleship (Matt 10:16).

DOVE, n. — A fowl of the order Columbæ, the genus Columba. The species are numerous. In scripture, a symbol of peace, of the Holy Spirit, and of the meek and innocent disposition.

TURTLEDOVE, n. — A species of dove; in scripture, the bird of the offering of the poor (Lev 12:8; Luke 2:24).

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 8:10-11 — "And he stayed yet other seven days; and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark; And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth."

Matthew 3:16 — "And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him."

Matthew 10:16 — "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves."

Song of Solomon 2:14 — "O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The dove-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the over-extension of the Holy-Spirit-as-dove imagery into doctrinal claims Scripture does not make (treating the dove-form at Christ’s baptism as a permanent or essential identification of the Spirit with the dove)—and by the loss of the rich multi-register biblical use of the dove across Noah, Christ’s baptism, Song of Solomon, the poor’s offering, and the disciple’s harmlessness.

expand to see more

The over-extension of the Holy-Spirit-as-dove imagery has, in some traditions, treated the dove-form at Christ’s baptism as a permanent or essential identification of the Spirit with the dove. The biblical text is more careful. The Spirit descended at Christ’s baptism in a bodily shape like a dove—a one-time visible manifestation whose dove-form was theologically significant (gentleness, peace, the heavenly origin, the new-creation echo of Noah’s dove) but not the Spirit’s essential or perpetual form. The Spirit subsequently descends on Pentecost as of fire—a different visible form serving a different theological purpose (the burning purification of new-covenant inauguration). The Spirit is not essentially identified with either dove or fire; both are bodily-shape manifestations chosen for theological significance at particular biblical moments. The recovery is the recovery of careful biblical attention to the actual claims of the text, without the over-extension that fixes the Spirit’s identification with a single visible image.

The deeper loss is the rich multi-register biblical use of the dove. The contemporary preacher often knows only one or two of the dove-references (Noah’s dove with the olive leaf; the Spirit-dove at Christ’s baptism) and is unaware of the wider biblical pattern: the dove of the Song of Solomon, the poor’s offering of two turtledoves, the wise-with-harmless dove of Matt 10:16, the dove-imagery of Hosea and other prophets. Each carries distinct theological substance, and the cumulative pattern is one of the richer bird-metaphors in Scripture. The recovery is the recovery of the wider biblical use: the dove of post-judgment peace (Noah), the dove of new-creation inauguration (Christ’s baptism), the dove of covenant intimacy (Song of Solomon), the dove of the poor’s accessible worship (Levitical offering), and the dove of disciplined harmless witness (Matt 10:16). The whole biblical dove-doctrine is far richer than the typical contemporary preaching exposes.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yōnāh (dove, including turtledove) and tōr (turtledove); Greek peristera (dove)—an extensive biblical bird-metaphor covering Noah’s flood-narrative dove, the Holy Spirit’s descent at Christ’s baptism, the beloved of the Song of Solomon, the poor’s sacrificial offering, and the disciple’s harmless-with-wise disposition.

expand to see more

Hebrew yōnāh (H3123) — dove (33 OT uses; same word as the name Jonah).

Hebrew tōr (H8449) — turtledove (especially in sacrificial contexts).

Greek peristera (G4058) — dove (10 NT uses; Matt 3:16; 10:16; 21:12; Mark 1:10; 11:15; Luke 2:24; 3:22; John 1:32; 2:14, 16).

Greek trugōn (G5167) — turtledove (Luke 2:24, the offering of Mary).

Usage

"In her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off—Noah’s dove’s post-flood return is one of Scripture’s most enduring symbols of peace and renewal."

"The Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him—the Spirit’s visible descent at Christ’s baptism, inaugurating His ministry."

"Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves—Christ’s pairing of the dove’s harmlessness with the serpent’s wisdom for the disciple’s witness in hostile territory."
